metadata.title: Data sets for Dissecting the Phenotypic Complexity of Biofilm Development and Quorum Sensing in Salmonella enterica Serovars- Figure 2,3,4,5 and 6,7,8.
metadata.description:
## Description

This repository contains the raw and processed datasets supporting Figures 2–9 of the manuscript, “Dissecting the Phenotypic Complexity of Biofilm Development and Quorum Sensing in *Salmonella enterica* Serovars.”

The deposited material includes bacterial growth measurements, growth-associated area-under-the-curve calculations, crystal violet measurements of growth-normalised attached biomass, scanning electron micrographs and exploratory LC–MS/DIA proteomics outputs. Experiments were performed using three independent biological replicates unless otherwise stated. Technical replicate measurements were averaged so that each independent biological experiment contributed one value to the analysis.

The repository also contains the corresponding high-resolution figures and treatment, bacterial-strain and biological-replicate identifiers linking the deposited data to the manuscript.

### Figure 2: Concentration-dependent effects of C₈-HSL on bacterial growth

This dataset contains OD₅₇₀ measurements from the C₈-HSL concentration-response growth experiment involving *Salmonella enterica* serovars Enteritidis UCH, Typhimurium ST14028, Virchow NCTC 7437 and Typhimurium TA1537, together with *Escherichia coli* NCTC 10418.

Cultures were exposed to C₈-HSL at final concentrations of 0.05, 0.2 or 1.0 mM, with corresponding vehicle-matched bacterial controls. Treatment and control cultures were standardised to the same initial blank-corrected OD₅₇₀ of 0.05. OD₅₇₀ was recorded at 12 hourly time points from 0 to 11 h during incubation at 37 °C with shaking at 150 rpm.

Three independent biological experiments were performed for each condition. The deposited data include raw and background-corrected OD₅₇₀ measurements, replicate-level growth curves, trapezoidal area-under-the-curve values and descriptive growth parameters. Maximum OD₅₇₀, maximum hourly OD₅₇₀ increase and operational lag time are provided as descriptive measurements.

### Figure 3: Effects of exogenous AHLs and farnesol on bacterial growth

This dataset contains OD₅₇₀ measurements from growth-curve experiments involving *Salmonella enterica* serovars Typhimurium ST14028 and Enteritidis UCH.

Cultures were exposed separately to C₆-HSL, C₈-HSL, C₁₂-HSL or farnesol, each at a final concentration of 0.2 mM, together with the corresponding vehicle-matched bacterial controls. All treatment and control cultures were standardised to the same initial blank-corrected OD₅₇₀ of 0.05. OD₅₇₀ was recorded at 12 hourly time points from 0 to 11 h during incubation at 37 °C with shaking at 150 rpm.

Three independent biological experiments were performed for each condition. The deposited data include raw and background-corrected OD₅₇₀ measurements, replicate-level growth curves and trapezoidal area-under-the-curve values used for treatment-versus-control comparisons. Maximum OD₅₇₀, maximum hourly OD₅₇₀ increase and operational lag time are included as descriptive measurements.

C₄-HSL was assessed separately at 0.2 mM in serovars Typhimurium ST14028 and Enteritidis UCH. The corresponding C₄-HSL growth curves are associated with Supplementary Figure S1 rather than the main Figure 3 comparison.

### Figure 4: Concentration-dependent effects of AHLs and farnesol on growth-normalised attached biomass

This dataset contains bacterial-growth and crystal-violet absorbance measurements from static biofilm experiments involving *Salmonella enterica* serovars Enteritidis UCH, Typhimurium ST14028 and Virchow NCTC 7437, together with *Escherichia coli* NCTC 10418.

Cultures were treated separately with C₄-HSL, C₆-HSL, C₈-HSL, C₁₂-HSL or farnesol at final concentrations of 0.05, 0.2 or 1.0 mM. Treatments were added following the 24 h pre-treatment measurement. The cultures were then incubated for a further 48 h, and attached biomass was measured by crystal violet staining at the 72 h endpoint.

For each independent biological experiment, background-corrected crystal violet OD₅₇₀ was divided by the corresponding blank-corrected pre-crystal-violet bacterial-growth OD₅₇₀. For graphical presentation, the resulting growth-normalised attached-biomass index was expressed relative to the corresponding vehicle-matched bacterial control, which was set at 100%.

Three independent biological experiments were performed, with technical replicate wells averaged before analysis. The deposited files include raw bacterial-growth and crystal-violet OD₅₇₀ values, treatment-specific blanks, vehicle controls, biological-replicate growth-normalised indices, vehicle-relative percentages and the statistical-analysis outputs reported in the manuscript.

Crystal violet staining measures total attached material and does not independently distinguish viable attached cells, cellular attachment or extracellular-material retention.

### Figure 5: Effects of natural products on growth-normalised attached biomass

This dataset contains bacterial-growth and crystal-violet OD₅₇₀ measurements from static biofilm experiments involving *Salmonella enterica* serovars Typhimurium ST14028 and Enteritidis UCH.

Cultures were treated separately with aloe-emodin, epigallocatechin gallate, thymoquinone, crude garlic extract or crude turmeric extract, each at a final nominal concentration of 200 µg/mL. Treatments were added following the 24 h pre-treatment measurement. The cultures were incubated for a further 48 h, and attached biomass was measured by crystal violet staining at the 72 h endpoint.

Background-corrected crystal violet OD₅₇₀ was divided by the corresponding blank-corrected pre-crystal-violet bacterial-growth OD₅₇₀ for each biological experiment. The resulting growth-normalised attached-biomass indices were expressed relative to the appropriate vehicle-matched bacterial control, which was set at 100%.

Three independent biological experiments were performed for each condition. Technical replicate wells were averaged before calculation of the biological-replicate values. The deposited data include raw bacterial-growth and crystal-violet measurements, treatment-specific blanks, vehicle-control measurements, replicate-level growth-normalised indices and vehicle-relative percentages.

This experiment was treated as an exploratory natural-product screen. The results are presented descriptively as mean ± SD, and no inferential statistical significance is claimed for comparisons with the controls, between the treatments or between the bacterial strains. The concentration of 200 µg/mL was not confirmed as non-bactericidal or sub-inhibitory, and antimicrobial, metabolic or viability-related contributions cannot be excluded.

### Figure 6: Effects of quorum-sensing and comparator compounds on growth-normalised attached biomass

This dataset contains bacterial-growth and crystal-violet OD₅₇₀ measurements from static biofilm experiments involving *Salmonella enterica* serovars Typhimurium ST14028 and Enteritidis UCH.

C₈-HSL and farnesol were tested at final concentrations of 0.2 mM. Chloramphenicol, chlorhexidine digluconate and 2-furanone were tested at final concentrations of 200 µg/mL. Chloramphenicol and chlorhexidine were included as antibiotic and biocidal comparators, respectively.

Treatments were added following the 24 h pre-treatment measurement. The cultures were then incubated for a further 48 h, and attached biomass was measured by crystal violet staining at the 72 h endpoint.

Background-corrected crystal violet OD₅₇₀ was divided by the corresponding blank-corrected pre-crystal-violet bacterial-growth OD₅₇₀ for each biological experiment. The resulting growth-normalised attached-biomass indices were expressed relative to the appropriate vehicle-matched bacterial control, which was set at 100%.

Three independent biological experiments were performed for each condition. Technical replicate wells were averaged before analysis. The deposited data include raw bacterial-growth and crystal-violet measurements, treatment-specific blanks, vehicle-control measurements, replicate-level growth-normalised indices and vehicle-relative percentages.

This experiment was treated as an exploratory comparator-compound screen. The results are presented descriptively as mean ± SD, and no inferential statistical significance is claimed. Growth normalisation does not exclude bacteriostatic, bactericidal or other nonspecific contributions to the observed differences in attached biomass.

### Figure 7: Scanning electron microscopy of 72 h *Salmonella enterica* biofilms

This dataset contains scanning electron micrographs of 72 h biofilms formed by *Salmonella enterica* serovars Typhimurium ST14028 and Enteritidis UCH on sterile glass coverslips.

The conditions included untreated LB bacterial controls and treatment with C₈-HSL, farnesol, epigallocatechin gallate, turmeric extract, garlic extract, thymoquinone, aloe-emodin or chlorhexidine digluconate. C₈-HSL, farnesol, epigallocatechin gallate, thymoquinone, aloe-emodin and chlorhexidine digluconate were tested at final concentrations of 0.2 mM. Crude garlic and turmeric extracts were tested at final concentrations of 200 µg/mL. Treatments were present throughout the 72 h static incubation.

Biofilms were fixed using 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M cacodylate buffer and post-fixed in 1% aqueous osmium tetroxide. Samples were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series followed by acetone, air-dried overnight, mounted on aluminium stubs and sputter-coated with an approximately 20 nm layer of gold.

Images were acquired using a Zeiss Crossbeam 550 scanning electron microscope at 5 kV, a probe current of 1 nA and ×7,000 magnification. Ten micrographs were collected along a linear transect, with a lateral displacement of approximately 100 µm between consecutive fields. The manuscript composite contains one representative micrograph for each bacterial strain and treatment condition.

Approximate visible-cell or cell-equivalent counts associated with the displayed panels are descriptive image-based estimates. They should not be interpreted as viable-cell counts or colony-forming-unit measurements because individual cell boundaries could not always be distinguished within dense bacterial clusters and surface-associated extracellular material. The SEM observations were qualitative and were not subjected to inferential statistical analysis.

Figure 8: Effects of quorum-sensing molecules, natural products and comparator compounds on viable bacterial counts

This dataset contains colony-forming-unit measurements obtained after 6 h treatment exposure for Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis UCH and S. enterica serovar Typhimurium ST14028. Three independent biological experiments were conducted for each strain. Within each biological experiment, the vehicle control and all treatment conditions were prepared from the same standardised starting bacterial suspension.

The compounds tested at 0.2 mM were C4-HSL, C6-HSL, C8-HSL, C12-HSL, farnesol, epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), aloe-emodin, thymoquinone, 2-furanone and chlorhexidine digluconate. Garlic and turmeric extracts were tested at 200 µg/mL, and chloramphenicol was tested at 10 µg/mL. The reference vehicle control contained 1% (v/v) ethyl acetate.

Following treatment exposure, cultures were serially diluted ten-fold in sterile phosphate-buffered saline. Aliquots of 100 µL were spread onto LB agar and incubated at 37 °C for 16–24 h. Plates containing 30–300 colonies were used to calculate CFU/mL using the colony count, dilution factor and plated volume. Counts below 30 colonies were classified as too few to count, while counts above 300 colonies were classified as too numerous to count.

Because 0.1 mL of the 10⁻¹ dilution was the least diluted sample plated, the lower limit of quantification was 3.0 × 10³ CFU/mL. Chloramphenicol-treated cultures were below this limit in all three biological experiments. They were therefore reported as below the quantification limit rather than assigned a value of zero and were excluded from inferential analysis.

CFU/mL values were log₁₀-transformed before statistical analysis. Each strain was analysed separately using one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, with treatment as the within-experiment factor and biological experiment as the matched block. When the overall treatment effect was significant, two-sided Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test was used to compare each treatment with the ethyl-acetate vehicle control while controlling the family-wise error rate.

For graphical presentation, the principal panels of Figure 8 are displayed over an enlarged range of 8.0–10.0 log₁₀ CFU/mL to improve visual resolution of differences among the vehicle, AHL, natural-product and selected comparator conditions. Chlorhexidine and chloramphenicol are shown in separately labelled lower-count panels using a range of 3.15–7.5 log₁₀ CFU/mL. This restricted graphical scaling did not affect the statistical analysis, which used the complete quantifiable log₁₀-transformed dataset.

The deposited material includes the original colony counts across the dilution series, plate-count classifications, selected countable plates, dilution factors, plated volumes, calculated CFU/mL values, log₁₀-transformed values, replicate-level measurements, summary statistics, treatment preparation calculations, repeated-measures ANOVA results, Dunnett-adjusted p values and high-resolution versions of Figure 8.

Figure 1: Conceptual overview of selected regulatory relationships

Figure 1 is a literature-derived conceptual diagram rather than an experimental dataset. It summarises selected regulatory relationships associated with quorum sensing, stress responses, adhesion, motility and biofilm formation in Salmonella enterica. The diagram was created using BioRender.com, and selected regulatory relationships were compiled from SalmoNet2.

None of the genes, proteins or regulatory pathways depicted in Figure 1 was directly measured or experimentally manipulated in this study. The figure is included solely as a conceptual framework for interpreting the phenotypic experiments. A high-resolution copy is included in the deposited material for completeness.

Supplementary scanning electron micrographs

The supplementary material includes original-scale PNG versions of the representative scanning electron micrographs used to construct the composite SEM figure. The images show 72 h biofilms of S. enterica serovar Enteritidis UCH and S. enterica serovar Typhimurium ST14028 following incubation in untreated LB or exposure to C8-HSL, farnesol, EGCG, thymoquinone, aloe-emodin or chlorhexidine at 0.2 mM, or garlic and turmeric extracts at 200 µg/mL.

Each image is provided at its original resolution of 2048 × 1536 pixels without cropping, resizing, resampling or contrast adjustment. The complete instrument acquisition strip and embedded 1 µm scale bar have been retained. Images were acquired at 5.00 kV and ×7,000 magnification using the SE2 detector. The displayed field of view was 16.33 µm, and the recorded image pixel size was 7.975 nm.

The reported image-based counts represent estimates of visible cells or cell-equivalent objects within the displayed field. They are not CFU measurements and should not be interpreted as quantitative measurements of viable-cell numbers, biofilm thickness or total biomass.

Data interpretation

The growth, crystal violet and CFU datasets provide complementary phenotypic information. Optical-density measurements describe changes in culture turbidity, crystal violet staining measures total attached cellular and extracellular material, and CFU enumeration measures recoverable viable bacteria under the specified culture and plating conditions. None of these measurements independently establishes that the observed responses were mediated through SdiA or another specific quorum-sensing pathway.

The CFU experiment was conducted after 6 h exposure in liquid culture, whereas the crystal violet and SEM experiments assessed older surface-associated biofilms. The CFU results should therefore not be interpreted as direct measurements of viable cells within the 72 h biofilms. Comparisons across these assays should account for their different endpoints, incubation periods and growth conditions.

The natural-product and comparator-compound experiments were exploratory. Reductions in attached biomass may reflect bacteriostatic, bactericidal, metabolic or attachment-related effects rather than specific quorum-quenching activity. The marked reductions in recoverable viable bacteria following chlorhexidine and chloramphenicol exposure are consistent with substantial antimicrobial activity under the CFU assay conditions.

The CFU reference condition contained 1% (v/v) ethyl acetate. This control was vehicle-matched to compounds prepared in ethyl acetate. Comparisons involving aqueous chlorhexidine or crude extracts prepared using ethanol should be interpreted with consideration of their different preparation solvents unless corresponding water- and ethanol-matched controls were also included.

SEM observations provide qualitative evidence of treatment-associated differences in surface coverage, cellular distribution and biofilm-associated material. They do not independently quantify viability, biofilm thickness or extracellular-matrix composition. Image-based visible-cell estimates are descriptive measurements and are not substitutes for CFU enumeration
